header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
(Waheed Iqbal v. The State and another)
(Abid Hussain v. Yasir Irfan and another)
(Abid Hussain v. Waheed Iqbal and another)
body: SARDAR MUHAMMAD SARFRAZ DOGAR, CJ:- By this single judgment, we decide the Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, submitted by the learned Sessions Court in terms of section 374, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.P.C.”), for confirmation or otherwise of the death sentence awarded to appellant Waheed Iqbal as well as Criminal Appeals No. 412, 419, and 420 of 2022, as all four matters stem from a single judgment dated 24.11.2022 (“impugned judgment”), delivered by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Islamabad-West in Sessions Case No.10 of 2021 and Sessions Trial No.03 of 2022, arising out of FIR No. 621/2010 dated 22.10.2020, 2 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 registered for the offences under Sections 302, 324, 337-F(ii), and 34 PPC at Police Station Margalla, Islamabad.

2. Vide the impugned judgment dated November 24, 2022, appellant/convict Waheed Iqbal was convicted under Section 302(b) PPC for committing Qatl-i-Amd of Talib Hussain and sentenced to capital punishment of death, alongwith an order to pay compensation of Rs. 200,000/- to the legal heirs of the deceased under Section 544- A Cr.P.C. (or undergo six months simple imprisonment in default). Through the same judgment, learned trial Court acquitted Waheed Iqbal of charges under Sections 324 and 337-F(ii) read with Section 34 PPC, whereas, co-accused Yasir Irfan was acquitted of all charges under Sections 302, 324, 337F(ii), and 34 PPC by extending him the benefit of doubt.

3. The prosecution case, as recorded in the FIR is that few months before the occurrence a dispute arose between the complainant side and the family of accused persons over a wastewater/sewerage line said to run from a dairy farm towards the complainant's land. A quarrel followed, criminal cases were registered, and the matter was said to have been patched up through the intervention of respectable persons. Nevertheless, the earlier dispute nevertheless supplied a motive for the subsequent attack.

4. According to the written complaint, Exh.P.AA, on 22.10.2010 at about 9:30 a.m. a further altercation and shooting occurred in the village, as a result of which Aamir, Ejaz and Tariq Hussain sustained injuries. The complainant stated that the injured persons were taken to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences Hospital (“PIMS”). Allegedly, approximately at about 12:20 p.m., outside the Emergency Department of PIMS, nominated accused Yasir Irfan and Waheed 3 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 Iqbal confronted them and acting in furtherance of their common intention, accused Yasir Irfan fired at Aziz-ur-Rehman with his 30bore Pistol, striking him on the left side of the chest below the armpit, whereas Waheed Iqbal with his 9 mm pistol fired at Talib Hussain, striking him on the right side of the chest. Both the injured died subsequently.

5. The incident at PIMS, rather than the earlier village occurrence, is the immediate subject of FIR No.621/2010, registered on the written complaint of Abid Hussain (PW.10). Initial investigation was carried out by Sub Inspector Shafique Ahmed (PW-13), who collected four empty shells of 30-bore (Ex.PM/DA) and six empty shells of 9mm (Ex.PN/DB) from the crime scene. Due to prolonged abscondence of both nominated accused, proceedings under Section 512 Cr.P.C. were initiated on 18.10.2011, and both accused were declared Proclaimed Offenders (P.O.) on 28.05.2012. Nearly a decade later, co-accused Yasir Irfan surrendered to join investigation, while Waheed Iqbal was arrested on 08.10.2020.
6. The charge was eventually framed on 09.10.2021 under sections 302, 324 and 337-F(ii), read with section 34, P.P.C. The prosecution examined fourteen prosecution witnesses and two Court witnesses.
7. At the culmination of trial, learned trial Court passed the impugned judgment whereby accused Yasir Irfan was acquitted and Waheed Iqbal was convicted as noted above.

8. Being aggrieved, convict Waheed Iqbal assailed his conviction and death sentence via Criminal Appeal No. 412 of 2022. The learned trial court transmitted Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022 under Section 374 Cr.P.C. for confirmation of the capital sentence. Conversely, 4 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 complainant Abid Hussain instituted Criminal Appeal No. 419 of 2022 challenging the partial acquittal of Waheed Iqbal, and Criminal Appeal No. 420 of 2022 challenging the complete acquittal of coaccused Yasir Irfan.

9. Raja Rizwan Abbasi, the learned counsel for the convict Waheed Iqbal (appellant in Criminal Appeal No.412) and Yasir Irfan (respondent in Criminal Appeal No.420 of 2022), vehemently argued that the conviction is based on misreading and non-reading of the evidence, as the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. He contended that the complainant was not an eyewitness to the occurrence, as he was sitting in a van parked in the hospital parking area, and his presence at the scene and opportunity to witness the occurrence was doubtful. The ocular account was also alleged to be replete with material contradictions, improvements, and discrepancies. Learned counsel further pointed out that the injured witness, Ibrar Hussain, had been given up by the prosecution, although his testimony was material to the allegations of additional firing. He also emphasized that no charge relating to an attempt to commit Qatl-i-Amd was framed in respect of PW Tariq Hussain, who sustained no injury.

10. In respect of respondent Yasir Irfan, learned counsel submitted that the Investigating Officer had concluded that he was merely present at the place of occurrence and was not armed with any weapon. He had neither caused any injury nor participated in the commission of the offence, and his name was placed in Column No. 3 of the challan on account of his abscondence. Learned counsel argued that the CCTV footage produced by the prosecution did not establish his participation in the occurrence. He further relied upon the statement of Muhammad Umer Khan (CW-2), a member of the 5 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 Special Investigation Team (SIT), who stated nothing incriminating against Yasir Irfan. The acquittal of co-accused Yasir Irfan on the same set of witnesses was also relied upon by learned counsel for appellant Waheed Iqbal, while maintaining that the evidence against him likewise required careful scrutiny and did not warrant his conviction.

11. Learned counsel further assailed the recoveries and the preparation of the police documents, arguing that the recovery memos and other material had not been reliably prepared at the time and place alleged by the prosecution. It was contended that although 9mm pistol empties were allegedly recovered from the place of occurrence and their parcel was entered in the daily diary register, however, the parcel containing 30-bore pistol empties, which was subsequently introduced into the prosecution case, was not reflected therein. The alleged recovery of the empties and the subsequent recovery of a pistol, according to learned counsel, did not establish the appellant Waheed Iqbal’s connection with the fatal shot attributed to him. He further pointed out that PW Tariq Hussain was not shown on the scaled site plan and that plan, if accepted, would place Yasir Irfan inside the emergency ward of PIMS Hospital at the relevant time, whereas the occurrence was alleged to have taken place outside the emergency ward.

12. Learned counsel also highlighted material discrepancies regarding the preparation of the case record. Although the private witnesses attributed the preparation of material documents to the Investigating Officer (PW-13), however, both PW-7, Tasawar Abbas, Head Constable, and PW-13 admitted that the documents were actually prepared by Tasawar Abbas (PW-7). It was argued that these discrepancies cast serious doubt on the authenticity and 6 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 contemporaneous preparation of the recovery memos. Furthermore, the Investigating Officer failed to prepare an unscaled site plan indicating the place where the 30-bore pistol empties were allegedly scattered.

13. Lastly, learned counsel submitted that the complainant caused a firearm injury to Naeem, the brother of the accused, and that the present case was registered as a counterblast to the incident involving the complainant party. In view of the doubtful ocular account, material contradictions, questionable recoveries, discrepancies in the police record, absence of reliable corroborative evidence, and prosecution’s failure to establish the appellants' participation in the occurrence, learned counsel maintained that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. He, therefore, prayed that the appeal filed by convict Waheed Iqbal be accepted, the convictions and sentences be set aside, and he be acquitted of all charges by extending the benefit of doubt whereas appeals filed by the complainant Abid Hussain be dismissed.

14. Conversely, the learned Deputy District Public Prosecutor strongly controverted the assertions made by the defense and contended with vehemence that the prosecution has successfully established its case against both accused persons across all essential ingredients of the charged offenses, beyond any reasonable shadow of doubt. He further submitted that the grounds urged on behalf of the appellant Waheed Iqbal do not, ipso facto, erode or destabilize the intrinsic worth of the evidentiary material marshaled by the prosecution, which remains sufficiently cogent, credible, and untainted to uphold the conviction and sentence passed against him. 7 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 15. In respect of the connected matter, the learned Deputy District Public Prosecutor supported the stance of the complainant seeking reversal of the partial acquittal of Waheed Iqbal and complete acquittal of Yasir Irfan. He forcefully argued that the learned Trial Court fell into grave error by engaging in misreading and non-reading of the evidence on record, thereby misdirecting itself on material facts. He emphasized that the ocular testimony, being fully corroborated by medical evidence and prompt investigative steps, had unequivocally linked all the accused with the commission of the crime. However, the learned Trial Court, while departing from settled principles of safe evaluation of evidence in criminal matters, arrived at a perverse and arbitrary conclusion in acquitting Waheed Iqbal under Sections 324 and 337-F(ii) read with Section 34, PPC, as well as totally exonerating the co-accused Yasir Irfan. Such findings, being the result of glaring legal and factual infirmities, have caused a serious miscarriage of justice and are, therefore, unsustainable in the eyes of law.

16. In appeals i.e. Crl.Appeal No.419 & 420 of 2022, the appellant/complainant has challenged the impugned judgment to the extent that respondent Waheed Iqbal was acquitted of the charges under Sections 324 and 337-F(ii), PPC, and respondent Yasir Irfan was acquitted of all the charges. The principal grounds raised in the respective memoranda of appeal, stated collectively to the extent they overlap, are that the impugned judgment is contrary to the evidence available on record and is the result of misreading and non-reading of material evidence. The appellant/complainant has asserted that the prosecution produced credible, confidence-inspiring and incriminating evidence in support of its case, which was sufficient to establish the involvement of the respondents in the occurrence, but the learned trial 8 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 Court failed to appreciate the same in its true perspective. It has further been maintained that direct ocular evidence was available on record, attributing specific roles to the respondents in the occurrence at PIMS Hospital, Islamabad as a result of which both injured persons succumbed to their injuries. It has been averred that the learned trial Court failed to properly assess the evidentiary significance of these specific allegations and the material connecting the respondents with the commission of the offences. In particular, the appellant has questioned the acquittal of Waheed Iqbal of the charges under Sections 324 and 337(ii), PPC, contending that the impugned judgment does not satisfactorily explain the basis for discarding the prosecution case in respect of those offences, despite the evidence relating to the same occurrence.

17. It has further been pleaded that the prosecution examined three ocular witnesses, two of them sustained injuries in the occurrence, and that their testimony remained materially consistent despite crossexamination. The appellant/complainant has also relied upon the CCTV footage pertaining to the occurrence at PIMS Hospital, maintaining that the same constituted important corroborative evidence which was not properly appreciated by the learned trial Court. Another ground raised is that undue reliance was placed upon the allegedly adverse portion of the statement of Investigating Officer Ashiq Muhammad (PW.14), while the testimony of Court Witness Muhammad Umar Khan, which, according to the appellant/complainant, exposed material infirmities in the Investigating Officer’s version, was not duly considered. It has, therefore, been asserted that the ocular account, the CCTV footage and the testimony of the said Court Witness were required to be evaluated collectively, rather than in isolation.

9 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 18. The appellant/complainant has further assailed the impugned judgment on the ground that the findings recorded by the learned trial Court are speculative, founded upon an erroneous interpretation of the evidence and unsupported by a proper appreciation of the material circumstances. It has been maintained that the alleged discrepancies and deficiencies in the prosecution case were given undue significance, whereas the incriminating evidence against the respondents was overlooked or not given its due weight. The appellant/complainant has disputed the conclusion that the prosecution case was shrouded in material doubt and has contended that the evidence, when considered in its entirety, did not justify the acquittal of Yasir Irfan from all the charges or the acquittal of Waheed Iqbal from the offences under Sections 324 and 337(ii), PPC.

19. Lastly, it has been pleaded that, in the presence of what the appellant describes as convincing and credible evidence, the learned trial Court was not justified in extending the benefit of doubt to the respondents in the manner it did. On these grounds, the appellant/complainant has prayed that the impugned judgment be set aside to the extent of the challenged acquittals and that the appeals against acquittal be accepted in accordance with law.
20. We have heard the arguments and perused the record.

21. There is no cavil to the settled proposition that a conviction for qatl-i-amd must rest on evidence proving the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The burden is not discharged merely by establishing that a homicide occurred, that the accused had a motive, or that he was present in the vicinity. The prosecution must connect the accused with the criminal act through evidence that, considered as a whole, is 10 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 safe to rely upon. The gravity and irreversibility of the sentence require careful scrutiny before confirmation.

22. Exh.P.AA did not state that Tariq Hussain or Ibrar Hussain had sustained additional firearm injuries during the PIMS occurrence. At trial, the complainant/PW-10 enlarged the ocular account to include a further shot by respondent Yasir Irfan at Tariq Hussain and a shot by convict Waheed Iqbal at Ibrar Hussain, together with aerial firing. During cross-examination, PW-10/complainant admitted it correct that these additional details were not recorded in the complaint and in the earlier statements put to him during the course of crossexamination. Ch. Ejaz Ahmed/PW-11 and Tariq Hussain/PW-12 likewise admitted it correct that the additional shots now attributed to these persons were not recorded in their earlier statements. The first Investigating Officer Shafique Ahmad S.I/PW.13 also admitted it correct that the complaint Ex.P.AA did not mention an injured person at the PIMS occurrence other than the two deceased.

23. The additions were material because they changed the alleged sequence, number of shots and allocation of roles in a fast-moving shooting. They were not merely differences about peripheral wording. The prosecution was required to explain a genuine omission, but the witnesses' answers did not dispel the difficulty as the original version alleged one shot by each accused against a different deceased, while the expanded version added further injured persons and further shots. The trial Court was justified in being cautious about these additions. At the same time, their impact upon the original allegation concerning deceased Talib Hussain must be adjudged together with the evidence about opportunity to observe, video identification, and physical corroboration. These additions/improvements cannot be said to be mere omission, rather the same are prima facie, dishonest 11 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 improvements which undermined the credibility of prosecution witnesses. In case titled as “Muhammad Nasir Butt v. The State” (2025 SCMR 662), hon’ble Supreme Court declared improvements in respect of assigning specific roles to each accused as dishonest and that same create serious doubt about the veracity of their testimony. For ready reference, relevant paragraph is hereby reproduced as under:- “6. In their statements recorded at the trial, the complainant Zahid Amjad (PW-3), Muhammad Hamid Amjad (PW-4) and injured Muhammad Majid Amjad (PW-10) have made dishonest improvements for assigning specific role to each accused, which creates serious doubt about the veracity of their testimony and it is not safe to place reliance on their statements. Reliance in this regard is placed on the case of "Muhammad Jahangir v. The State"
(Emphasis supplied)

24. Furthermore, the evidence concerning the complainant's position when the shooting took place raises a substantial question. The scaled site plan (Exh.P.AB), was prepared by the draftsman on the pointation of PW-10/complainant. It shows the complainant at point No.6 sitting on the rear seat of his vehicle white Suzuki Carry Van and it also describes the hospital parking area between that point and point No.1 i.e. the alleged place of occurrence. The draftsman Malik Amir Shahzad/PW-8 admitted it correct that the site plan was prepared only on the complainant's pointation and that parking lay between the two points i.e. point No.1 and point No.6 and the distance between these two points, as mentioned by the draftsman is 40 feet. Ch. Ejaz Ahmad/PW-11 stated that Abid Hussain and Aashiq Muhammad were near the vehicle at the time. Tariq Hussain/PW-12, stated in cross-examination that Abid Hussain remained inside the vehicle, while they were looking for a suitable place to park. 12 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 25. There is neither a rule that a person inside or beside a vehicle cannot see an assault outside a hospital emergency entrance nor is the site plan, prepared on one witness's pointation, conclusive proof of every person's precise position. However, in a prosecution for a shooting alleged to have taken only a few seconds, these matters were central to the reliability of observation. The prosecution did not, in the reasons relied upon by the learned trial Court, establish a sufficiently precise and consistent placement of the PWs i.e. complainant, Tariq Hussain and Ch. Ejaz Ahmad relating to the stretcher, the entrance, the slope and the alleged shooters so as to resolve the concern about the line and duration of sight. The first unscaled site plan was not produced, and the scaled plan did not mark PW-12 Tariq Hussain's position. Tariq Hussain/PW-12 also stated that he had not supplied the draftsman with the precise details of the place of occurrence or pointed out the Yasir Irfan/shooter's position to him.

26. The learned trial Court noted a further inconsistency concerning the position of deceased Aziz-ur-Rehman on the stretcher. The witnesses uniformly placed him on the left side, whereas the scaled site plan, as described by Shafique Ahmed S.I/PW-13, showed him on the right. There was also evidence about a slope at the emergency entrance and uncertainty whether the alleged position of accused Yasir Irfan was inside or outside the emergency area. These discrepancies mainly affected the allegation against Yasir Irfan; nevertheless, they reveal that the physical reconstruction of the occurrence was not settled with the precision expected where two people were said to have fired at different victims amid confusion and movement in a hospital entrance. They also bear on how reliably the witnesses could assign an individual shot to each accused. 13 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 27. The Court does not reject PW-10 merely because he is the complainant, or PW-12 because he is related to him. The difficulty lies in the objective question of opportunity to observe the occurrence. The complainant's own placement, the parking area between him and the indicated point of occurrence, the unmarked locations of other witnesses, and the brief duration of the firing shown in the CCTV collectively leave a reasonable doubt about whether the witnesses could reliably distinguish and assign the particular shot that struck deceased Talib Hussain to convict/appellant Waheed Iqbal.

28. Another important aspect of the matter is that the prosecution relied on footage from the PIMS Emergency entrance, described in the trial record as USB P-1 and clips P-2/1-23. Malik Safdar Khalid/PW-6, the PIMS security supervisor, stated that, after obtaining permission from a senior officer, he accompanied the first Investigating Officer to the CCTV control room. An operator obtained the footage from the DVR and copied it to a USB, which the Investigating Officer received under memo of recovery (Exh.P.E); the footage/clips were also secured under memo of recovery (Exh.P.J). The operator who actually selected and exported the footage was not examined, according to the account set out in the impugned judgment. PW-6 also admitted that the DVR's displayed time was not always accurate.

29. The description of the footage in PW-6's evidence was that a person wearing a lawyer's uniform was using a mobile telephone; two stretchers then appeared; a person in white Shalwar Kameez carrying a pistol in his right hand moved towards the stretchers and fired; people began running; and the person in the lawyer's uniform remained occupied with the telephone as the firing began and then disappeared from the camera's view along with others. The footage 14 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 thus has probative value to show that a person apparently holding a pistol fired near the stretchers. The crucial question, however, is whether it identifies that person as Waheed Iqbal or not?. The judgment does not identify the person in white Shalwar Kameez by facial features, a distinctive item of clothing, testimony from someone familiar with the recording, or any other reliable identifying characteristic. Nor does the fact that an unidentified person in white Shalwar Kameez is seen firing establish that the person was Waheed Iqbal merely because he was named in the FIR. The footage depicts the act of firing; on the evidence described, it does not independently establish the identity of the actor. The case law titled as “Ishtiaq Ahmed Mirza” (PLD 2019 SC 675), lays down the relevant considerations in assessing authenticity and reliability of the Video/footage. Even if the recording is accepted as a genuine record of what its camera captured, it cannot serve as corroboration identifying Waheed Iqbal as the person firing when the image does not itself identify him. The established principles of criminal jurisprudence dictate that where facial identification is obscured or unidentifiable, it is legally unsafe to base a conviction solely upon a partial admission or a general physical similarity, in the absence of a formal expert facial recognition/comparison report or robust corroborative circumstantial evidence. Consequently, the prosecution's case against the appellant on the primary charge of murder remains unproven. In this respect reference can be made to cases reported as “Muhammad Ramzan and another v. The State” (2025 SCMR 1742) and “Fazal Mehmood and another v.The State through PG. Sindh and another” (2026 SCMR 350).

30. The next aspect of the matter is alleged Crime empties, recovery memos and the alleged weapon of offence. The prosecution 15 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 asserted that four crime empties of a 30-bore pistol and six crime empties of a 9 mm pistol were collected at the place of occurrence under recovery memos Exh.P.M and Exh.P.N. Its case was that the 30-bore pistol was used by accused Yasir Irfan and the 9 mm pistol by appellant/convict Waheed Iqbal. Yet the case property produced in evidence comprised six 9 mm empties, P-10/1-6, and only two 30bore empties, P-11/1-2. The learned trial Court was unable to reconcile the discrepancy between the four 30-bore empties allegedly seized and the two produced at the time of evidence. Although that discrepancy most directly concerns the prosecution's allocation of the 30-bore pistol to Yasir Irfan, however, it calls for a careful examination of the seizure records and custody of the parcels as a whole. CW-1 Ahmed Nawaz 537/HC, who is Moharir Malkhana of Police Station Margalla, could not explain how one parcel of crime empties was available when register No.19 at serial Nos.548/549 reflected two separate parcels. He admitted it correct that the parcel produced in Court did not bear the stamp 'SA'. The evidence of complainant/PW-10 and Tassawar Abbas 5235/HC (PW-7) also raised questions about who prepared the recovery memos as PW-10 said that the contents of Exh.P.N were already written when he signed it whereas, PW-7, Tasawar Abbas, admitted it correct that almost every document prepared during the investigation was in his handwriting and specifically stated that he had prepared the recovery memos. Surprisingly, PW-7 was not included among the companions named in the first Investigating Officer's evidence in respect of arriving at PIMS. PW-10's statement as a witness to collection of the empties was, in his own statement during cross-examination, recorded during the later SIT proceedings in 2021 rather than contemporaneously. These matters are more than minor discrepancies in spelling or form; 16 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 they concern the time, authorship and integrity of the primary seizure documents.

31. The first Investigating Officer further stated that Talib Hussain died at about 8:50 p.m. but admitted it correct that he had been described as 'deceased' in the first police diary, which he said was made before 3:00 p.m. The 30-bore empties were also absent from entry No.54 of the daily diary register dated 22.10.2010. These circumstances do not, by themselves, prove that every police document was fabricated, yet, their significance is cumulative for the reasons that the prosecution relied upon the recovery of the empties to distinguish the alleged roles and weapons, while the record discloses inconsistencies in the number of empties, parcel seals, register entries and the claimed preparation of the recovery memos.

32. In addition to above, it is worthwhile to note here that no reliable ballistic comparison linking the six 9 mm empties attributed to Waheed Iqbal with the pistol later recovered from him is identified in the trial Court's reasons or in its summary of the evidence. The later recovery occurred on 16.10.2020, approximately ten years after the PIMS occurrence, when Waheed Iqbal allegedly produced a pistol from an unused washroom in his house during the subsequent investigation. If, for the sake of discussion, it is admitted that he got the alleged recovery effected during the course of investigation, even then, in the absence of a demonstrated ballistic link and a dependable chain connecting the relevant crime empties to the scene, mere possession of an unlicensed pistol in 2020 does not establish that it was the weapon used to kill Talib Hussain in October-2010. Therefore, the same cannot be said to have decisive corroborative force in this murder charge.

17 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 33. In “Khair Muhammad” (2025 SCMR 1599), the Hon’ble Supreme Court treated flaws in the collection and dispatch of crime empties and the absence of a dependable link between physical evidence and the accused as matters capable of generating reasonable doubt. The factual setting of that case is not identical, and the decision is not applied mechanically, however, the present concern is that the seizure material relied upon to corroborate Waheed Iqbal's identity is itself affected by unresolved custody and documentation questions, while no dependable firearm-comparison result is shown to bridge the gap. These recoveries cannot safely be used to transform uncertain identification into proof beyond reasonable doubt.

34. Now, adverting to the next important aspect worth discussion i.e. Medical evidence, alleged withholding of witnesses and absence of other corroborative evidence. The medical evidence confirms that both deceased sustained fatal firearm injuries. It is consistent, at a general level, with the prosecution's allegation that shots were fired at PIMS. However, it is trite law that medical evidence is mere supportive/confirmatory type of evidence; it can tell about locale, nature, magnitude of injury, duration of the injury and kind of weapon used for causing injury but it cannot tell about identity of the assailant who caused the injury; therefore, it can neither provide any corroboration nor be of any help to the prosecution in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case. Guidance has been sought from the cases of “MUHAMMAD RAMZAN versus The State” (2025 SCMR 762) and “IMRAN versus The STATE” (2026 SCMR 47); relevant portion from the latter case law is hereby reproduced as under: - “8. Insofar as the medical evidence is concerned, it is by now well settled that the medical evidence is only supportive evidence, which may confirm the ocular account with regard to receipt of injury, nature of the injury, kind of 18 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 weapon used in the occurrence but it would not identify the assailant. Reference in this context may be made to the cases of "Muhammad Tasaweer v. Hafiz Zulkarnain and 2 others" (PLD 2009 Supreme Court 53), "AltafHussain v. FakharHussain and another" (2008 SCMR 1103) and "MursalKazmi alias Qamar Shah and another v. The State" (2009 SCMR 1410).”
(Emphasis added)

35. Furthermore, the prosecution's account of additional injuries also remained medically uncertain. Dr. Farrukh Kamal (PW-9) recorded seven injuries on Tariq Hussain and stated, in response to the request for medical opinion, that it was impossible to assess which wounds had been received on the same day. The MLC of Tariq Hussain was not part of the challan as a complete document; an attested page was tendered later. The witnesses attributed a left-hip injury to Yasir Irfan, yet the injury described in the medical evidence as corresponding was Injury No.4 i.e. an exit wound of 1.5 x1.5 cm irregular averted margins bloodstained left gluteal region. The prosecution did not obtain a proper declaration concerning injuries Nos. 5 to 7. These matters substantially impair the reliability of the additional shots narrative and are relevant to the complainant's appeal against the acquittal under sections 324/337-F(ii).

36. The complainant (PW.10) alleged that Ibrar Hussain sustained a firearm injury on his left arm by appellant Waheed Iqbal. However, he was not produced at trial, even though an injury statement had been prepared during the initial investigation and his evidence was capable of addressing the additional shot attributed to Waheed Iqbal. The trial Court recorded that the prosecution failed to prove the charge under sections 324 and 337-F(ii) because injured Ibrar Hussain was not produced. Although, his absence does not by itself determine whether Waheed Iqbal fired at Talib Hussain, but it leaves the further alleged shot without testimony from the person said to have sustained it. The 19 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 prosecution did not provide a satisfactory evidentiary basis for treating the later account of multiple shots as reliable corroboration of the core allegation.

37. The learned trial Court, in impugned judgment also recorded that three hospital guards/chowkidars were examined during investigation but were not called as prosecution witnesses. It is not an inflexible rule that a prosecution must call every witness who may have seen an occurrence, and the non-production of an independent witness does not automatically make the private witnesses untrustworthy. In the peculiar circumstances here in this case the shooting was alleged to have occurred at the Emergency entrance of a busy hospital, the prosecution itself secured CCTV footage, and independent guards were said to have been identified as potential witnesses. Their absence assumes significance in combination with the disputed opportunity of the complainant to observe, the short duration of the recorded firing, and the absence of reliable video identification of Waheed Iqbal. Article 129, illustration (g), of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, permits (but does not compel in every case) an inference that evidence which could be produced and is withheld would, if produced, be unfavourable to the party withholding it. The Court does not treat non-production of the guards as independently conclusive; rather, it is an additional factor when assessing whether the prosecution has excluded reasonable doubt. This lends credence to the view that despite availability of best evidence with the prosecution, it did not produce the same because had said evidence been produced, the same would have gone against the prosecution’s narrative. Reliance is placed on “Mst. Saima Noreen v. The State” (2024 SCMR 1310), “Muhammad Nasir Butt v.The 20 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 State” (2025 SCMR 662) and “ZunairYounas v.The State” (PLD 2026 SC 222).

38. So far as the motive is concerned, the sewerage-line dispute provides a possible motive and is not treated as absent, however, the existence of prior hostility does not resolve the crucial question of identity of Waheed Iqbal. The record also discloses the earlier criminal case concerning a serious firearm injury to Naeem, Waheed Iqbal's brother, for which members of the complainant party were implicated. This earlier hostility is a circumstance that could explain the prosecution's theory and at the same time makes it necessary to assess the risk of over-attribution carefully. The prosecution still had to prove that Waheed Iqbal was the person who fired the fatal shot, to which the prosecution has been miserably failed.

39. The convict/Waheed Iqbal's prolonged absence from the process of law is a circumstance that may be considered, but abscondence is not substantive proof that he committed the alleged murder. It can lend support to an otherwise established prosecution case, however, it cannot replace the evidence necessary to establish the act and his identity. In this case, the prosecution has failed to establish the case against Waheed Iqbal, therefore, mere his abscondence alone is not sufficient to maintain conviction. In case titled as “Rafaqat Ali alias Foji and another v. The State and others” (2024 S C M R 1579), the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that “mere absconsion is not conclusive proof of guilt of an accused. It is only a suspicious circumstance which cannot take place of proof and its value depends on the fact of each case. Mere absconsion of an accused cannot be made basis of conviction. Absconsion of an accused, being a relevant fact, can be used as a corroborative piece of evidence but cannot be read in isolation and has to be read along with 21 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 the substantive pieces of evidence. Abscondence can never remedy the defects in the prosecution case as it is not necessarily indicative of guilt. Moreover, abscondence is never sufficient by itself to prove the guilt.” Even otherwise, when a person is named as a murderer in a case, whether rightly or wrongly, he usually becomes scared and tries to conceal himself in order to avoid possible police torture and detention, therefore, mere abscondence of an accused by itself is not sufficient to maintain his conviction and sentence in absence of other reliable evidence. Reliance in this regard is placed on case laws titled as “Laiq Shah v. The State”(2026 SCMR 257) and “Imran v. The State”(2026 SCMR 47)

40. The cumulative assessment of above noted circumstances is that the case of prosecution is replete with circumstances which cast reasonable doubt in respect of Waheed Iqbal’s identity being shooter as alleged in this case. At the risk of repetition, firstly, the complainant's position in or beside the vehicle, the intervening parking area, the inconsistent placement of witnesses and stretcher, and the absence of a reliable site reconstruction leave material uncertainty about his opportunity to see and attribute the shot. This factor is not decisive alone, but it materially weakens the asserted certainty of the identification. Secondly, the three central witnesses materially improved/expanded the account of the hospital shooting with additional shots and injuries that were absent from their earlier statements, and those expansions are not supported by a consistent medical account. Thirdly, the CCTV shows a person firing but, it does not visibly identify appellant Waheed Iqbal. The questions of recording's provenance, time and safe custody were not fully resolved. Fourthly, the physical evidence relied upon as corroboration is affected by discrepancies in the number of empties, the sealing and 22 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 custody of parcels, the preparation of memos, and the absence of a demonstrated ballistic match to the pistol later recovered from the appellant Waheed Iqbal. It is trite that in order to extend benefit of doubt to an accused, it is not necessary that there should be several circumstances creating doubt, rather one reasonable doubt is sufficient to acquit an accused. Reliance is placed on the cases reported as “Rasheed Ahmad alias Seeda v. The State” (2026 SCMR 798), “Muhammad Siddique and another v. The State and others” (2026 SCMR 783), “Laiq Shah v. The State” (2026 SCMR 257), “Mushtaq Ahmed v. The State” (2026 SCMR 60), “Maqsood Alam and another v. The State and others” (2024 SCMR 156), “Abdul Qadeer v. The State” (2024 SCMR 1146), “Muhammad Imtiaz Baig and another v. The State through Prosecutor General, Punjab, Lahore and another” (2024 SCMR 1191), “Muhammad Hassan and another v. The State and others” (2024 SCMR 1427), “Khial Muhammad v. The State” (2024 SCMR 1490) and “Muhammad Ijaz alias Billa and Another v. The State and others” (2024 SCMR 1507).

41. Consequently, the appeal against conviction (Criminal Appeal No. 412 of 2022), succeeds and is allowed. The conviction of Waheed Iqbal under section 302(b), P.P.C., and the sentence of death and consequential compensation order founded upon that conviction cannot be sustained thus, the same are hereby set aside. The death sentence is NOT CONFIRMED and reference is answered in NEGATIVE.

42. Coming to Criminal Appeals No.419 and 420 of 2022 concerning Yasir Irfan’s acquittal of all charges and acquittal of Waheed Iqbal in remaining charges i.e. 324, 337-F(ii) of PPC. 23 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 43. The learned trial Court recorded reasons for acquitting Yasir Irfan which were based on evidence on record rather than mere assumption. The CCTV description places a person in lawyer's uniform using a mobile telephone immediately before and as the firing began; the person shown firing is a different, unidentified figure in white Shalwar Kameez. As per testimony of Shafique Ahmad S.I (PW-13) respondent Yasir Irfan was not shown firing and was also not captured opening the alleged fire shot at deceased Aziz-ur- Rehman. The latter Investigating Officer, Ashiq Muhammad S.I (PW- 14), stated that upon review of the CCTV footage and the investigation record, respondent Yasir Irfan was neither armed nor shown to have fired, and he was placed in column No. 3 of the challan because of his presence and abscondence. The complainant himself admitted awareness of those investigative findings and that he did not challenge the same through a private complaint or an application for transfer of investigation. The Court is mindful that the view of the police is not binding, however, its relevance lies in the fact that the prosecution did not produce sufficiently strong contrary evidence to displace it on the issues discussed by the learned trial Court.

44. The learned trial Court also considered that respondent Yasir Irfan was a practising lawyer and his brother Naeem was admitted to PIMS with a serious fire arm head injury arising out of the earlier village occurrence, making his presence at the hospital explicable independently of the alleged murder. It noted the lack of proved calldata records despite their collection during investigation, and the absence of evidence reliably establishing a prior telephonic conspiracy or common intention. The veracity of allegations that the alleged injury sustained by Tariq Hussain attributed to Yasir Irfan was affected by the uncertainty of the medical record, the mismatch record 24 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 between the ocular account and the documented exit wound further cast doubt on the prosecution’s case. The discrepancy between four alleged 30-bore empties and the two produced, together with the doubts about their seizure and custody, further impaired the prosecution case against respondent Yasir Irfan.

45. So far as the ground of the appellant/complainant that the witnesses remained firm in cross-examination and that two of the ocular witnesses were injured is concerned, the medical record relating to injured Tariq Hussain does not reliably establish the alleged injury at PIMS or its attribution to respondent Yasir Irfan. The video does not show respondent Yasir Irfan’s firing. The prosecution's own latter investigation did not establish that he fired the shot, and the complainant did not produce reliable corroborative evidence sufficient to overcome those deficiencies. Mere presence at the hospital, a prior family dispute, and a period of abscondence do not establish participation or common intention beyond reasonable doubt. The learned trial Court assessed the visual account, the medical material, the recovery evidence, the result of the later investigation and the explanation for respondent Yasir Irfan's presence. The conclusion that the prosecution did not prove Yasir Irfan's involvement is a reasonable view of the evidence. It has not been shown to be perverse or to result from grave misreading or non-reading of evidence. The double presumption of innocence therefore remains operative.

46. The complainant's second appeal against acquittal concerns Waheed Iqbal's acquittal under sections 324 and 337-F(ii), P.P.C. The learned trial Court found established that the prosecution did not produce injured Ibrar Hussain, the person said to have received a firearm injury on his left arm from Waheed Iqbal during the PIMS occurrence. That finding went to the very proof of the injury and 25 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 attribution necessary for the additional charges. The case was not one where the trial Court ignored a produced injured witness; the person alleged to have sustained the relevant injury was not brought into the witness box.

47. In addition, the first written complaint made no mention that Tariq Hussain or Ibrar Hussain was injured by further shots at PIMS. The further shots emerged in later testimony and were confronted with the earlier statements. The complete MLC was not part of the challan and an attested page was produced only later. The earlier and later stances, therefore, did not establish with reliable precision that a separate firearm injury was inflicted by Waheed Iqbal during the PIMS occurrence. These were rational grounds for the learned trial Court to distinguish the additional counts from the core allegations concerning deceased Talib Hussain.

48. The ground of complainant that all charges had to rise or fall together is not correct as it is trite that each charge must be proved on its own ingredients and supporting facts. A specific allegation in the original complaint against Waheed Iqbal concerning a fatal shot fired at deceased Talib Hussain did not establish, without reliable proof, the separate and later-added allegation that he also fired shot at Ibrar Hussain. The complainant has failed to prove that the acquittal from the offences under sections 324/337-F(ii) was perverse, arbitrary, or founded upon grave misreading or non-reading of evidence.

49. It is well settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that acquitted accused enjoys double presumption of innocence, one before the trial of the case and second after his acquittal and acquittal cannot be interfered without any strong and exceptional reasons which are lacking in the instant case. Reliance is placed on case law titled as 26 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 “Basharat Ali Chaudhry v. Sabir Ali and others” (2026 SCMR 1527). In case titled as “Altaf Yousuf v. The State through Additional Director FIA, Passport Circle, Karachi and another”(2026 SCMR 1390), It has been held as under:- “8. The philosophy innocent until proven guilty is the fundamental vade mecum and golden thread to the doctrine of presumption of innocence as a shield but not as a sword. The presumption of innocence is not mere legal theory but it is in fact evidence in favour of the accused and starting point with the assumption that the accused has not committed any crime, but this powerful shield is not impenetrable come what may. Rather, it can be subjugated if the prosecution produces irresistible and credible evidence to meet high standards of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. This principle is every now and then recapitulated on the strength of a Latin maxim ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat (burden of proof lies with the one who declares, not the one who denies). The presumption of innocence is considered as the foundation stone of administration of criminal justice. The globally settled jurisprudence in the criminal justice system including our own country fervently and overwhelmingly espouses the principle innocent until proven guilty considering it the basic limb or component of fair trial opportunity and due process of law rather than preferring or declaring an accused guilty before proven innocent , which seriously undermines the fundamental principle of fair trial/due process and obviously the presumption of innocence.

9. An acquittal is called a "double presumption of innocence" and it is not mandatory that there must be numerous aftermaths that give rise to doubts to justify the benefit to the accused, rather a single circumstance if creating reasonable doubt is enough to enable him a benefit. The interference in a judgment of acquittal is found to be rare unless some glaring errors of law and fact are shown by the prosecution to demonstrate that the acquittal judgment is perfunctory with shocking conclusion. In the criminal justice system, if two sensible and judicious conclusions can be drawn, then the view which espouses and provides backing towards acquittal must be subscribed to. The Court in an appeal against acquittal would not ordinarily interfere but gives due weightage to the findings of acquittal which carries a double presumption of innocence, i.e. the initial presumption that an accused is innocent until found guilty, which is then fortified by a second presumption once the Court below confirms the assumption of innocence. The learned High Court while reversing the acquittal did not advert to any cogent or solid ground for its reversal and remanding the matter to the Trial Court after a long period of time. No independent application of mind seems to have been applied to evaluate the Trial Court order but the acquittal order was set aside in a slipshod manner without scrutiny of record or incriminating material, which if at all or at the best, available for indictment of the petitioner who was acquitted in both the cases.”

Reference can also be made to case law titled as “Muhammad Fareedon Rehman v. The State and another” (2026 SCM R 987) 27 | Murder Reference No. 14 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos. 412, 419 and 420 of 2022 50. Consequent upon above discussion, criminal Appeals No.419 &420 of 2022 are, DISMISSED and acquittal of respondents Yasir Irfan and Waheed Iqbal is maintained.

51. The conviction warrant and all consequential process, to the extent founded upon the conviction and sentence now set aside, shall stand recalled and cancelled in accordance with law. The compensation order under section 544-A, Cr.P.C., being consequential to the conviction now set aside, is also vacated. Waheed Iqbal shall be released forthwith if not required to be detained in any other case. Yasir Irfan's acquittal is upheld and shall remain operative. The jail authorities shall be informed promptly of the result of the appeal No.412 of 2022 of Waheed Iqbal and reference.
52. The record of the trial Court, together with a copy of this judgment, shall be transmitted back to the learned Trial Court forthwith, in accordance with law.
